newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU row over single currency sets stage for summit.
newsitem.headline: EU row over single currency sets stage for summit.

text.p: The European Union was set for an 11th-hour showdown on Thursday over economic discipline after the introduction of a single currency.
Finance ministers from the 15-nation bloc were to meet in a special session (1600 GMT) in Ireland's capital on the eve of a two-day summit of EU leaders.
They were to try to agree a pact that will keep countries' economies on the straight and narrow after the introduction of the euro on January 1, 1999.
At issue is a German demand that countries in a single currency bloc should be fined for running excessive budget deficits and that there should be only clearly defined exceptions.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said again on Thursday he would insist when meeting his EU colleagues that his proposed stability pact for the euro should have clear penalties and verifiable definitions for exceptions.

"I will not move away from the clear stability goal. Every member state must know what the consequences are if it diverges from the stability path and lets its budget deficit go over three percent," he said in a prepared text for parliament.
Officials, however, were optimistic that agreement could be reached. Financial markets were keen to see whether the single currency was still on track.
"I am confident that we will find a solution that will show all citizens the determination of the European Union to create a euro with long-term stability," German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said.
The stability pact is a key element of a report on economic and monetary union (EMU) due to be studied by EU leaders at the summit proper, which begins on Friday.

Other aspects of the report have already been informally agreed. They include the legal basis for the euro and a new post-EMU exchange rate mechanism to keep EU currencies outside the euro bloc stable.
The EU leaders were also to discuss at the summit the bloc's long-term future, in the shape of a draft EU treaty written by the Irish EU presidency.
"We must demonstrate a commitment to advance the political and economic health of the Union," John Bruton, Irish prime minister and summit host, said in a letter to his colleagues on Wednesday.

The Irish draft treaty shows the majority of countries are heading towards closer cooperation in crime fighting, joint employment policies, stronger foreign policy links and a true border-free Europe with common asylum and immigration policies.
It also calls for the EU to create by 2001 a vast area of freedom, security and justice that ensures the free movement of people.

Of all the leaders coming to Dublin, British Prime Minister John Major will be among the most watched. With his ruling Conservative party torn apart over Europe, Major will be under pressure not to appear too conciliatory to his EU colleagues.
Britain opposes most of the proposals under dicussion for the draft treaty -- which is supposed to prepare the bloc for enlargement into central and eastern Europe.
London also has an opt-out on the single currency, making discussions on post-EMU life something of a political minefield for the embattled British leader.
